item.title: From Help Center article to decision-making experience
item.content:encoded:
e-learning

Working closely with marketing stakeholders, I helped transform pricing information into a dedicated decision-making experience for future learners, balancing discoverability, content strategy and conversion goals.

Freelance Product Designer

Freelance Project

2026

Context

As part of a freelance project for Skoove, I worked on designing a dedicated pricing experience for web visitors. At the time, pricing information for logged-out users was primarily accessible through a Help Center article. While existing customers could view subscription options after signing in, prospective users had limited visibility into plans, pricing and subscription benefits directly on the website.

This created an interesting gap between discovery and decision-making. Users could find Skoove through search engines, articles and marketing pages, but understanding the value of a subscription often required additional steps before reaching the actual purchase flow.

Side-by-side comparison of the existing pricing page available to logged-in users without a premium subscription and the Help Center pricing article (logged-out experience).

Pricing existed,
but the pricing experience didn't

One of the first things I mapped was the journey for non-premium users. Accessing subscription plans required creating an account, signing in and navigating through several screens before reaching the pricing interface.

At the same time, many visitors arriving from Google were landing on a Help Center article listing prices as plain text. The information was technically available, but the experience lacked context, comparison, trust signals and clear paths forward.

Current user flow showing how non-premium users navigated from landing page to subscription purchase.

One of the most impactful changes was also one of the simplest: introducing a dedicated Pricing entry in the website navigation, making subscription information accessible without requiring users to create an account first.

Designing for discovery and decision-making

The brief was not simply to create a pricing page. The page needed to serve multiple purposes at once:

  • Help visitors understand Skoove's plans and subscription options.
  • Communicate value beyond price alone.
  • Answer common objections before purchase.
  • Improve discoverability through SEO and emerging AI-powered search experiences.
  • Create a clearer path from interest to trial.

This shifted the project from being a pricing exercise into a broader information architecture challenge.

From wireframe to final structure

The PM proposed an initial wireframe for the page structure, which became our starting point. From there, I proposed a new structure for the hero, based on benchmarking the pricing pages of ChatGPT, DocuSign and Miro on desktop and mobile. Two patterns stood out: bringing the pricing cards into the hero, fully visible within the screen height on desktop, and placing the CTA before the list of benefits, so it doesn’t get lost. I then designed new pricing cards built on Skoove’s UI kit, borrowing details like a label on the highlighted plan and a soft background separating the price from the benefits.

On mobile, the PM initially wanted the pricing cards in a carousel. Using the same references, where all three stack their plans vertically, I made the case for stacking the cards one below the other instead: a carousel would hide important information behind an extra interaction, while stacked cards only ask users to scroll. That’s the version that went live.

Benchmarking ChatGPT, Miro and DocuSign pricing pages on desktop and mobile.

A pricing page is more than pricing

Many of the design decisions focused on reducing uncertainty.

Plan comparisons, benefit-oriented content, social proof and FAQs were introduced to address common questions before they became blockers.

The project also explored how visual storytelling could support the messaging. Early concepts for the feature illustrations were developed as part of the design process, helping communicate the learning experience beyond pricing alone. The final artwork was later refined by Skoove’s in-house design team.

The page became less about displaying subscription tiers and more about helping visitors make an informed decision.

Early layout explorations, marketing proposals and annotated design iterations showing how the page structure evolved.

Final pricing page design highlighting plan comparison, benefits, FAQs and conversion-focused sections.

Extending the design system

The project introduced several new web components and required updates to existing navigation patterns. These changes were later incorporated into the Web UI Kit, helping establish more consistent experiences across marketing and product-related pages.

New components created for the project and later integrated into the Web UI Kit.

Notes

One of the most interesting aspects of this project was seeing how closely content, discoverability and product design intersect. The challenge wasn’t creating a new subscription system, but making an existing one easier to find, understand and trust.

Adding Pricing to the main navigation made subscription information easier to discover before sign-up.

As an external designer, I didn’t have access to performance data after launch. Because the pricing page was a new experience, there was no behavioural baseline to compare against. The natural measure of its impact is the change in free trial starts and converted users.

See the live pricing page

Sometimes the challenge is not designing a new feature. It’s making an existing experience easier to find, understand and trust.

item.title: Designing growth experiences at Mondly
item.content:encoded:
e-learning

My role at Mondly involved a variety of tasks, collaborating closely with designers, marketers, User Acquisition and Growth specialists, website developers, and data scientists to consolidate Mondly's rebrand across all touchpoints.

Senior Product Designer

Fully remote

2023 - 2024

About Mondly

Mondly is a language learning app that aims to make language learning fun and easy through technological innovation and multiple language combinations.

In 2022 Mondly was acquired by Pearson, giving the Product team a chance for a big redesign of Mondly’s platform and web presence.

My Role at Mondly

My role sat between Product Design and Growth. I designed growth and monetization experiences, and the variants for A/B tests that the Growth and User Acquisition teams set up and analysed. Testing the old vs. the new design helped us validate the rebrand with data and plan the marketing transition.

Before I joined the team, the product designers put in place a detailed design system that served as base for all the future assets we developed on the way. I collaborated closely with one of my colleagues on the creation of a style guide in Notion, where we documented the details of the New Mondly Brand and its usage.

View of some of the components built for the Styleguide in Figma

Balancing Growth with Brand Experience

A recurring challenge at Mondly was balancing short-term acquisition goals with the long-term product experience.

The User Acquisition team often looked to high-converting apps like Temu or AliExpress for inspiration. These apps rely on urgency, aggressive promotions and visually dense interfaces. The patterns clearly worked for them, but we in the Product Design team felt they could hurt trust in a learning product and didn’t fit Mondly’s brand.

Instead of rejecting the requests, I looked at why those patterns convert: urgency, a clear offer and high visibility. I then designed Limited Time Offer banners that used those principles within Mondly’s design system.

From inspiration to adaptation: keeping the conversion principles, leaving out the visual density.

For the Valentine’s Day campaign, this meant taking the energy of high-conversion promotions and translating it into Mondly’s visual language. It took several rounds of feedback with Marketing, Growth and User Acquisition. I explored different versions, explained the trade-offs of each, kept what supported their goals and adjusted what compromised the brand.

Explorations for the Valentine's banner: timer in a header vs. inside the card, offer-first vs. campaign-first, and the weight of the CTA. The final kept the timer inside the card with a full-width CTA.

The same approach shaped the Limited Time Offer banners that appeared in the app outside seasonal campaigns. Here, instead of debating which direction was right, we tested three variants in an A/B/C test and let user behaviour decide.

Mondly Web & Marketing

With a major rebranding underway, we created brand guidelines based on our design system that we could extend into marketing materials. We conducted a series of A/B tests to compare the performance of the new design versus the old one, ensuring a positive impact on user engagement.

Redesigned Offer page

For this project, we adapted the app’s design system for use on a marketing landing page for the first time. This laid the foundation for a scalable design system tailored to web marketing materials, evolving with the team’s needs. It also enabled us to expand the style guide specifically for marketing designers, who would use it in areas such as social media campaign ideation.

Before: Mondly's old Offer page design. After: Redesigned Offer Page on iPad mini and iPhone SE

The redesigned Offer page resulted in an increase in average time on page and a lower bounce rate compared to the original control version.

App Store & Google Play images

In order to test the impact of the rebranding on the Stores, we initiated a project to extend the new brand to these images. The light mode was introduced after benchmarking research showed competitors favoring light backgrounds in their App Store images. We organized several Design Team workshops to develop a light version of our new brand, allowing us to include it in the A/B testing.

Screenshots of the dark and light versions of the App Store images for iPhone X

Data showed a nearly 3% increase in App Store downloads with Mondly's Light theme version compared to the control and dark theme variants. With this percentage we met our OKRs for Q1 2024

Seasonal Campaigns

Seasonal campaigns such as Spring Sale, Valentine’s Day and Black Friday were one of Mondly’s key growth initiatives. They encouraged free users to upgrade to Premium through limited-time offers, and they followed a consistent in-app conversion flow.

In-app conversion flow for seasonal campaigns.

The Challenge

3D illustrations were a core part of Mondly’s visual identity. Each campaign needed a new illustration from an external 3D artist, followed by several rounds of stakeholder review.

The quality was excellent, but as campaigns became more frequent, this process slowed down launches and made it hard to get new creative directions approved.

The previous workflow depended on a bespoke 3D illustration for every campaign.

Rethinking the Approach

While designing the Spring Campaign, I discussed the workflow with the Design Lead. We realised the bottleneck wasn’t the layout, it was the dependency on a new 3D asset every time.

So we changed the question:

How can we keep Mondly’s 3D visual identity while making campaigns faster to produce and easier to align on with stakeholders?

I redesigned the campaign layout so the 3D look came from an AI-generated background instead of a bespoke illustration. The designer in charge could now produce the final asset in-house, without waiting on an external partner, while the campaign still felt unmistakably Mondly.

The background was generated with Midjourney, using a defined prompt for the style and image size so results stayed consistent across campaigns. Because the brand was still evolving through everyone’s work, we first validated the images with the Product Design team in our weekly fresh eyes sessions, especially with the Design Lead, before showing them to stakeholders. This removed the round-trip with an external 3D artist: we could iterate on the visuals ourselves and bring stakeholders an option that was already aligned with the brand.

Spring Campaign redesign: an AI-assisted background keeps the 3D look without a bespoke illustration.

Validation

We aligned with stakeholders to test two variants with different backgrounds against the original campaign in an A/B/C test.

Variant B performed best, with 7% more Activate taps than the original campaign. The new layout showed that faster, in-house production could keep the brand experience and improve engagement at the same time.

The new layout became the template for the following seasonal campaigns, so each new promotion could be produced in-house and tested without commissioning new 3D artwork.

Learnings

  • Growth requests are signals, not specs. Asking why a pattern converts let me keep the principle (urgency, a clear offer, visibility) without hurting trust in a learning product.
  • Remove the bottleneck, not the quality. Campaigns were slow because of the dependency on bespoke 3D artwork, not because of the layout. Reframing the problem made production faster and improved engagement.
  • A design system can scale beyond the product. Extending it to the Offer page, store images and campaigns gave marketing and growth a shared foundation.
  • Let data settle the debates. My first time working in user acquisition taught me to turn opinions into testable variants.

item.title: Improving ecommerce flows at EyeEm
item.content:encoded:
e-commerce

I worked at EyeEm for 2+ years on the browser-based platform and the Webflow marketing site. When the team shrank, I partnered with the PM to hire new product designers, reviewing portfolios and interviewing candidates together.

Product Designer

Berlin, Hybrid

2021 - 2023

About EyeEm

EyeEm is a photography community and marketplace that facilitates connections between creators and prominent brands to source original and on-brand content.

My role at EyeEm

I was one of the designers in the Product team, working on the browser-based platform. I led the Cart & Checkout redesign, working with a PM, the Data team and a front-end developer, and I maintained EyeEm’s Webflow marketing site.

Project status: the redesign was in its final review before development when EyeEm went through insolvency, so it never shipped. I'm sharing it for the process: diagnosing drop-offs with data, prioritising quick wins and designing within an existing system.

Reducing friction in the purchase journey

The redesign started from funnel data prepared by the Data team and shared by the PM, which showed where users were dropping off between the Cart and a completed purchase.

From there, we identified pain points, formed hypotheses and proposed improvements, including background color inconsistencies, premature tax calculations and SSO issues for logged-out users. We also consulted the legal team on changes like pre-saving billing and payment details.

The company was under pressure, so we needed to move fast and effectively. We prioritised by impact vs. effort, favouring changes that were also low effort for front-end development. I ran fresh eyes sessions with the two other product designers to review the work, and the final design was a consensus between the PM, Data, Front-End and me, with input from several areas of the company.

Identifying Data take-aways and UI pain points on the Cart & Checkout flow

Screenshot from the user flow analysis in Figma

UX Exploration

Cart Page

With a 60% drop-off rate among logged-out users before reaching the authentication step, we wanted to identify the main pain points on the Cart page.
Top Navigation

The Cart page lacked EyeEm’s familiar top navigation, which could make users feel as though they’d left our site, potentially impacting trust. We hypothesized that reintroducing the top navigation might improve user confidence and retention.

VAT Calculations

VAT calculations were appearing too early in the cart flow. As users added more items, the displayed total rose significantly, which might discourage them. We considered moving VAT calculations closer to the payment step to present a more approachable total earlier in the process.

Dark Theme vs. Light Theme

A previous designer’s audit had already flagged parts of this flow as outdated. Looking at the screens in depth, we found that the Cart had no top navigation and used a light background, which could make users feel they had left EyeEm. Benchmarking how competitors handled their carts supported this hypothesis.

Switching to EyeEm’s dark theme was also a low-effort quick win: it was our main theme, and all the components already existed in the design system and UI kit.

Introducing more payment methods: Long term goals

To enhance convenience, we considered adding more one-click payment options, such as PayPal, Apple Pay and Google Pay, in future iterations.

Authentication for logged out users

Approximately 15% of users were dropping off on the Authentication screen. We required logged-out users to log in or create an account before proceeding, but this interruption often disrupted their flow.
Authentication Modal

To create a more seamless experience, we moved authentication to a modal, allowing users to keep their Cart in view while logging in or signing up.

UX writing

To keep users engaged, we explored updating our UX copy with clearer instructions, gently reminding users they were in the middle of a purchase.

Guest Checkout: Long-term goals

We also discussed the potential for a Guest Checkout, allowing users to skip authentication until later stages. While this feature wasn’t implemented in this iteration, it remains a consideration for the future.

Checkout Page

Only 10% of users who reached the Checkout page completed their purchase, highlighting a need to streamline this stage. We aimed to compress the steps required and reduce user interactions.
Cart Preview & Buy Now button

Previously, the “Buy Now” action was hidden in the second step and often inaccessible with longer Cart lists. We standardized the Cart preview by grouping items by license type, which kept the “Buy Now” option in view, encouraging quicker decision-making.

Transfer Licensing

Many of our users—often designers or agencies buying for clients—needed an option to transfer licensing directly to their clients. Previously, they had to call Support to complete this transaction. By adding this feature to the redesign, we streamlined the process and responded to a frequent user need.

Pre-save payment and billing information: Long term goals

To streamline the purchase process, we considered pre-saving user data, such as cart details and billing information. However, due to capacity and alignment with the legal team, we decided to prioritize this feature for future iterations

Thank you Page

Dark Theme Consistency

To maintain a cohesive user experience, we applied EyeEm’s dark theme to the Thank You page as well. This ensured visual continuity throughout the checkout journey, reinforcing a sense of familiarity and completion. Introducing a light theme at this final stage could have disrupted the flow and made the experience feel disconnected from the rest of the platform.

EyeEm’s Web presence

EyeEm.com combines the flexibility of Webflow with the capabilities of front-end development, giving designers complete control over the UI and behavior of some areas of the website. I maintained various site areas and launched around four landing pages per quarter for marketing campaigns, collaborating with the Marketing and Innovation teams. I was responsible for ideation, design, implementation, and final release of these projects.

Here are some live examples:

eyeem.com

eyeem.com/magazine

eyeem.com/awards

creativetrends.eyeem.com

Learnings

  • Data makes a problem concrete. The funnel numbers turned a project with many opinions into a shared diagnosis, and helped align the PM, Data and Front-End on what to fix first.
  • Quick wins live inside the system. Reusing the dark theme and existing components made improvements cheap to build when speed mattered most.
  • Define success at the start. We had the baseline funnel data, so measuring the impact after launch would have been straightforward, but we never agreed on targets. Today I’d set them at kick-off.

item.title: Designing Interactive Product Experiences for Life Sciences
item.content:encoded:
SaaS

BaseCase is a no-code platform that helps life sciences companies transform complex healthcare data into interactive product experiences. I gradually moved into UX/UI Design, creating client-facing tools, product documentation, and interactive demo applications that made complex workflows easier to understand.

UX/UI Designer

Berlin

2017 - 2020

About BaseCase

BaseCase is a no-code platform used by life sciences companies to transform spreadsheets into digital applications for medical communication, product education, and sales enablement.

My role at Basecase

I joined BaseCase as a Marketing Designer, working directly with the Design Manager, who was also part of the software team and had led design until then. Our first project was redesigning the print materials for trade fairs, with one flyer per product add-on. Without calling it that at the time, we were building a small design system to keep the website and print materials consistent.

When I was asked to cover a demo app for a client, the CEO suggested I keep producing them. There was a lot to do: besides creating new demos, many older ones needed to be redesigned and updated as BaseCase’s features evolved. That’s how I became responsible for the Demo App Library.

Complex software doesn't need more documentation, just better explanations.

The Demo App Library

My main responsibility was building a growing library of interactive demo applications used to communicate complex product capabilities and healthcare workflows.

The Demo App Library was a growing collection of interactive applications showcasing BaseCase’s capabilities—from onboarding and feature walkthroughs to complex healthcare use cases.

I owned the end-to-end process, from understanding the brief and designing the experience to building the applications inside the BaseCase platform.

The demos were used by Marketing at events and in campaigns, and many were also part of the product documentation, linked from Jira tickets.

Design Workflow

1
Understand the product feature and target audience
2
Explore concepts and wireframes in Sketch
3
Create a fictional healthcare brand and visual identity
4
Build the interactive experience in BaseCase
5
Test internally and iterate
6
Deliver for QA and documentation

Because their scope was purely illustrative, the demos used fictional healthcare brands instead of real clients. When Marketing wanted to reach a specific group of clients, I adapted a demo’s brand to that audience.

Close-ups to some of the tools that made part of the Demo App Library

Marketing Assets

Beyond product experiences, I designed marketing visuals supporting feature launches, trade fairs and website content. Many of these illustrations were created for the BaseCase Features pages, helping communicate complex product capabilities through simple visual examples.

Example of some of the Feature illustrations created for BaseCase's website

Learnings

  • This is where I learned UX/UI. Building demos taught me to turn complex features into experiences people could understand at a glance.
  • Systems before they had a name. Keeping the website, print materials and demos consistent showed me the value of reusable patterns early on.
  • Maintenance is part of the job. As the product evolved, so did the demos. Updating old ones mattered as much as creating new ones.
